item.title: Extracting and Classifying Geospatial Expressions Using Large Language Models: A Case Study of Urban Planning Documents
item.description:
Majid Hojati, Rob Feick
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70429
ABSTRACT Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) present new opportunities to advance text‐based analyses, particularly for identifying and disambiguating geospatial information expressed as natural language text. This study explores the capabilities of an LLM to identify, classify, and spatially query geospatial expressions found in urban planning documents. Urban planning encodes regulatory information, domain expertise, and local knowledge, much of which is geographic in nature, in reports and plans. Interpreting this geographic information is challenging for professionals (e.g., planners and lawyers) and community members. This paper presents an automated pipeline developed to assess an LLM's ability to extract geospatial expressions, determine their relevant spatial scale (micro, meso, and macro), and to identify urban features referenced by a specific development proposal. Three types of planning documents were examined from a mid‐sized city (Kitchener, Ontario, and Canada), namely a City‐authored Official Plan (OP), private consultants' development proposal reports, and transcripts from public meetings. A hierarchical Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) model processed text to extract explicit and implicit geospatial expressions, and a multi‐agent architecture converted these expressions into SQL queries against municipal data layers. Performance varied systematically by expression type and document type. The model handled implicit expressions best in the public‐meeting transcripts but performed poorly on explicit expressions in property‐specific reports. On a paired comparison, the pipeline outperformed two established geoparsing tools (GeospaCy and Mordecai3) on locally‐grounded planning documents. While this work illustrates how LLMs could automate interpretation of urban planning documents, the approach could also be applied to other application contexts where geospatial references are encoded in text forms.

item.title: A Basin‐Wise GLOF Susceptibility Assessment in the Western Himalayas: Integrating Remote Sensing‐ GIS and Multi‐Criteria Decision Analysis
item.description:
Rayees Ahmed, Anil V. Kulkarni
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70443
ABSTRACT Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) pose an increasing threat to high mountain environments across the world, especially in the Himalayas where climate change is accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost degradation. This study presents a detailed GLOF susceptibility analysis of the western Himalayas covering five major river basins, ie Satluj, Chenab, Jhelum, Beas, and Ravi by integrating high‐resolution remote sensing data with a multi‐criteria decision‐making approach. A detailed inventory of 1573 glacial lakes was developed using manual delineation of Sentinel‐2A and LISS‐IV images. Forty‐eight potentially dangerous lakes were identified based on size and dam composition. Following the guidelines of NDMA and GAPHAZ, 12 important physical and geomorphic parameters were selected and evaluated using Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with the addition of Cumulative Weightage Technique (CWT). AHP Analysis indicated that 20 lakes were high hazard, 23 lakes were medium hazard, and five lakes were low hazard. The basin‐wise analysis revealed that Satluj and Chenab are particularly vulnerable owing to the presence of large and fast‐growing lakes. A temporal assessment of 48 selected potentially dangerous lakes from 2000 to 2024 revealed a 115% increase in total lake area, highlighting their rapid expansion under a warming climate. The susceptibility framework was validated using seven historical GLOF events, all of which had hazard scores > 0.7, in agreement with the high susceptibility lakes identified in this study. The study recommends that detailed field investigations be carried out on high‐hazard lakes including bathymetric surveys, assessments of moraine stability, and real‐time monitoring to validate remote sensing findings and to inform early warning systems. This approach offers a transferable and policy‐relevant framework to support GLOF risk mitigation and climate adaptation planning in glacierized regions. This study relies primarily on remote sensing data, and uncertainties in lake identification and the lack of field validation may affect susceptibility classification.

item.title: A GIS‐Based Method to Prioritize Railway Links for Climate Resilience Planning Based on Operational Exposure
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Conventional climate risk assessments typically consider hazard, exposure, and vulnerability dimensions, but often restrict exposure to spatial hazard intersections, neglecting the operational intensity of infrastructure. This study proposes a geographic information systems (GIS)‐based framework that uses operational exposure derived from freight and passenger flows as the primary metric for network prioritization. By integrating origin–destination matrices with spatial infrastructure topologies, the methodology calculates distinct exposure profiles. An adjustment factor is introduced for high‐speed rail (HSR) corridors to reflect their strategic importance. Application to the Turkish national railway network demonstrates that peak operational exposure is spatially clustered along primary HSR segments (e.g., Ankara‐Eskişehir), which mathematically surpass maximum‐capacity conventional logistics arteries. The proposed data‐driven spatial framework provides a scalable and transferable approach for preliminary network screening, establishing an operational baseline for subsequent integration with probabilistic climate hazard and infrastructure vulnerability assessments.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

Conventional climate risk assessments typically consider hazard, exposure, and vulnerability dimensions, but often restrict exposure to spatial hazard intersections, neglecting the operational intensity of infrastructure. This study proposes a geographic information systems (GIS)-based framework that uses operational exposure derived from freight and passenger flows as the primary metric for network prioritization. By integrating origin–destination matrices with spatial infrastructure topologies, the methodology calculates distinct exposure profiles. An adjustment factor is introduced for high-speed rail (HSR) corridors to reflect their strategic importance. Application to the Turkish national railway network demonstrates that peak operational exposure is spatially clustered along primary HSR segments (e.g., Ankara-Eskişehir), which mathematically surpass maximum-capacity conventional logistics arteries. The proposed data-driven spatial framework provides a scalable and transferable approach for preliminary network screening, establishing an operational baseline for subsequent integration with probabilistic climate hazard and infrastructure vulnerability assessments.
